text: [h1]SUMMARY[/h1]  [Conceptualization] : It's that one Role-Playing Game that emphasis on "Role-playing" with text-heavy amazing narrative, interesting setting and enticing plot. Gameplay relies mostly on skill check system through dialogues and exploration to help the protagonist investigate the murder case and maybe even investigate about himself.    [b]Setting... and what is this game about?[/b]  [Encyclopedia] : You play as amnesiac drunk detective stranded in a place called Revachol. The "disgraced former capital of the world, divided into zones of control under foreign occupation -- half a century after a failed world revolution". Apparently there is a gruesome murder case going on. This might or might not tie to the protest going in the street and the state of decaying town going on around.  [Shiver] : And that's your job. As a detective, you roam around, feel the wind blow through the city with a withering rundown village, a doomed commercial area that might be cursed or not, a mysterious church and someplace full of containers. The world might not be as big as other open world game. But it's fully packed with contents   [b]Detective game? Open-world RPG?[/b]  [Logic] : Apparently. As this game emulate tabletop RPG. While you are investigating you will face a lot of obstacles in form of "Skill check" and your character's skills determine your chance of success. For example if you are thinking of some solution with given information if you put more point into me, Logic, you will be more likely to figure it out.  [Endurance] : But even failure is kinda fun in this game. If you want to read some painful but funny (and sometime to the point of black comedy) it's fun to fail in a while.  [Half Light] : Do save. Save a lot. This game (at least on normal mode) let you save anywhere. Save many. Save before it's too late.   [b]What and Who we are investigating?[/b]  [Inland Empire] : "Crime of a century" that might result in great darkness looming over Revachol.  [Empathy] : People of Revachol... might remind you a lot of people in real world.  [Inland Empire] : What is even "real" what are you talking about?  [Empathy] : Shhh... hang on Inland I'm talking about characters of this game. They are mostly people who has been through the stage of today's politics in real world. You can... mostly feel them. This is why many people love this game. Proximity. Human touch. They have been through "loss business" "falied romance" "loneliness" "poverty" "disastrous miscommunication" "not enough to pay rent" and did I mention "poverty"?  [Rhetorics] : And... you see? in this game even your skill check argue with each other sometime.   [b]So this game is "political" ?[/b]  [Drama] : Forbidden word in today's gaming huh? I might say everything is and could be political. But in the end I feel that it's more philosophical ...and everything is philosophical  [Rhetorics] : Political. I even don't like some part of what's seemingly problematic about it. But it's one of a few game where you could have serious discussion about economy with NPC, serious discussion about other aspect of society, and life, and Art... don't forget ART  [Drama] : Hard... of core  [Suggestion] : So while it has next to no combat, you fight and convince people with words. It's wordy but in a good way. There might be some skill check on exploration like could you hear or see something? could you jump from one place to another or could you catch something blowing in the wind? if you can it's pretty cool. How can one not want to play as cool character.  [Volition] : And even if you fail them it's still cool. Comedic Cool.   [b]Are there Perk or customization?[/b]  [Encyclopedia] : Yes. This game also contain equipments system that will change your Stats/Skills until unequiped. Drug and Drink that temporary boost/reduce your stats. And "Thought Cabinet" that act like "Perk/trait" in other games they let you internalize some "concepts" you have learnt depend on how you approach things.   [Logic] : So that's mean your choices in role-playing effect your character building to certain extent.   [b]How about bugs or accessibility issues in this game?[/b]  [Interfacing] : During initial launch I've face with some minor inconvenient bug about window/fullscreen mode but they fix it later in patch, good work. Other than that the control feel fine.  [Perception] : Also the interface seem confusing a first as I don't know if we can restore health/morale from clicking above number if healing items presented, left me wonder where have my healing items gone in inventory.   [b]Now... on to the aesthetics[/b]  [Conceptualization] : What to say you can see how much people praised this games as art. It's storytelling combinded with it's visual art style alone are enough to declare it's art.  [Suggestion] : And even if you don't care about art. It's still a fun game on it's own. It's not overly detach from player's experience as "high" art or something like that  [Hardcore Aesthetic] : It's "people" art  [Conceptualization] : Music are great too. "Red Rock Riviera" (OST on street outside of cafe scene) is very iconic it reflex a lot of the story about long gone fleeting moment of glory and only nostalgia left. While my favorite, The song from fishing village offer some dim hope and beautiful sorrow at the same time.  [Pain Threshold] : Still. As a person with Tinnitus (constant ringing in the ears). I've find container scene's music annoying to the point of almost painful. I feel they tone it down in some later patches. But I think it's not  agood idea to have tinnitus-like sound in the videogame in the first place.   [b]To sum it up again...[/b]  [Esprit de Corps] : It's a game where you roleplay as a detective be it ART detective, Cool Visual-scan deduction detective, Forget-your-gun detective, bad cop, good cap, funny cop, boring cop, poor cop, mega rich (wannabe) cop, Apocalyptic cop etc.  [Suggestion] : And oh... Disco Detective!  [Inland Empire] : Yes it's about Disco after all... Disco... [spoiler]and broken hearts.[/spoiler]

TLDR: Is gud game, go buy 15 copies of it.

text: This one is special.  Imagine someone threw D&D, L.A. Noire, Eastern European post-communism, and the movie Inside Out into a blender.  Now imagine that such an absurd mix not only came out well enough but that it somehow works brilliantly.  It's hardcore.  HARDCORE TO THE MEGA!  Here's how the magic works, much like Planescape: Torment, you wake in a mysterious world that you remember nothing of, except it's a world sort of similar to ours, an alternative post-Cold War mess of a decaying world, and you ought to explore it.  Everyone is ready to point out that you are a pathetic excuse for a cop, an alcoholic, fan of bad music, and incapable of doing anything right.  Yet, you remember nothing, there's a murder case to solve, and a polite (but eager) sidekick who wants you to do so.  And that's when the fun begins: are you going to be a good cop, or a neoliberal clown who torments the locals for bribes, or maybe an artistic moralist who's having a hard time distinguishing between reality and fiction?  Or a combination of all of these?  Or something entirely different?  That's the beauty of it, as it makes you role-play hard to figure out your character's place in this strange world that isn't ours.  As you go on about your business, your mind is constantly trying to help you, except you're such a mess that every aspect of you is now a character with its own voice and personality, admonishing you, or giving you hints, or just wasting your time.  And your choices many times depend on how friendly you are with those aspects of yourself.  Literally, as you will be putting "skill points" into the voices in your head, hoping they will help you get out of a bad situation, or provide you with enough panache that you will smooth talk some random person into opening themselves to you and reveal their secrets.  Those are your objectives: talking to people and see where that takes you.  The choices are yours and every conversation is a complex battle of wits between whatever you're trying to be, the people who loathe your existence, and whatever aspect of your own mind decided to get in the way this time.  Interactions with major characters can turn into actual boss fights as your words fail to do enough damage, or maybe they parry a hit just when you needed.  It's truly a dramatically affair, with a bizarre presentation, and an engaging narrative, all of which combine into a completely unforgettable experience.  The art style, an aesthetic that reminds you of an old oil painting full of tiny details to find is just gorgeous.  The music, subtle, memorable, and (more importantly) appropriate for every moment.  It is not perfect, because nothing is, but I will be hard-pressed to point out its occasional flaws -- the experience supercedes it all.  But enough about that, as there's tare to pick on the ground, just behind those two drunks up ahead, and you just know that if you don't get enough money soon you will be spending the night out in the streets and finally go completely insane.

text: Just finished the game after 60 hours of gameplay and I don't really know what I can say to express how ecstatic I feel about this game. The writing is superb and admirable for its sheer scope alone; the game world is one of the most interesting fantasy worlds I have seen in a while, and it's so densely packed with history and politics that it really feels alive; and the art direction is just ... well, it really tickles my Art Cop brain.  So instead of continuing to gush over this game, I'll give you some advice instead in case you're also thinking about playing it: 1) Take your time. Don't just skip through dialogues, really take in all the information you get. The game rewards you for paying attention and saying the right things at the right time. (It really helps that, with the Final Cut version at least, the game if fully voiced.) 2) Keep an open mind. The game bombards you with all sorts of strange ideas from minute one, and it doesn't spend a lot of time explaining these ideas (which makes sense given the premise of the game). Take it all in and think about what it all means *to you*, and I think you can get a lot out of the experience. 3) Don't save scum. This one is a bit hypocritical because I ended up doing just that for large portions of my playthrough. But looking back I wish I would've done less of it. Failure is a big part of the game's narrative and some truly amazing things can come out of you completely messing up a critical skill check. Just learn to let go and see where the game takes you instead of going back and aiming for that perfect outcome. Believe me, there is no perfect outcome.  And that's it. I hope this game will bring you as much joy as it did me. :-)

text: I downloaded this game expecting a Sherlock Holmes-esque mystery thriller. What I got was a lethal dose of human experience. Politics. Suffering. The detective work is a vessel facilitating intimacy and conversation. A nihilistic world, burning in the flames after leaping from the frying pan. At the epicentre of chaos; a man who has forgotten trauma, unwittingly using his condition to gaze at the world with a juvenile, somewhat healed perspective. A man vulnerable to proselytism from all angles. A man that can completely embody the choices you make as a player; a world that can echo these sentiments. Disco Elysium is incredible and I would recommend it to anyone who can withstand some reading.

text: [b]Disco Elysium[/b] is a game that comes out once in a lifetime. It may be just me enjoying melancholic stories of broken individuals in a dying world, but in my humble opinion, this one is the best narrative role-playing experience on the market ever. Yes, even better than legendary [b]Planescape: Torment[/b]. This game should be in a vocabulary next to the definition of the "Role-playing game". I've never experienced anything like it in terms of storytelling, character- and worldbuilding, and I sincerely believe that I never will again. It reminded me of [i]"Filth" by Irvine Welsh[/i] 'cause no other game made me laugh out loud and think of killing myself at the same time so often. So, if you don't mind heavy depressing vibes and reading 90% of your playtime then you should definitely try this one out, bratan/chica. I wish I had more free time and a shorter backlog of unfinished games to play this one more than once.

text: One of the best games I have played, if not THE best.  You are doing yourself a disservice by not playing it.   It's emotional. It's otherwordly funny. It actually has something to say. It's (and I mean it) deep.  It's also beautiful, both visually and in terms of the story, however bleak the setting may seem.  It may not be a feel-good game, and there are a lot of heavy topics explored (and flawlessly so). It is by no means a fantasy fulfilment, and it never tried to be. Even the game mechanics show that you cannot be everything, nor can you be the best all the time. You have to chose. You have failed, and you will fail again. You have hurt others, you are always running the risk of hurting them again, and vice versa.  And you have to, somehow, find a way to go on.  Or not.   Obvious as it is, this game touched me tremendously. And not even on a level that most games do, in form of being sad a while and then moving on. Or contemplating something for 5 minutes and then calling it a day. No, this is something different. This game has the capacity to strip you of your beliefs and putting them under a microscope. You may just find that you are a hypocrite, or that you have believed something naive, and not in the game world, but in the real one.   And this is ultimately the amazing link this game has with the real world. It's just just fantastic *enough*, but it constantly calls back to this world through big or small references. Myself I spotted quite a few call-backs to my own nation's culture, and even though they were never the focus, they did still make me think.  This game presented an opportunity to think about how real world history is told, who actually creates it, and who gets to tell and manipulate it later. And who in the end suffers from that manipulation.  It never preaches, though. In the end, you decide everything; who or what to believe, what to make of the world. Up to you to find a reason to carry on.  It is not the ending that stood with me the most, it was the ENTIRETY of the game. text: The Disco Elysium controversy centers on a bitter legal and corporate battle over the game's intellectual property (IP) and creative control, following the sudden departure of its original creators from studio ZA/UM in late 2021 and early 2022.  Robert Kurvitz, Aleksander Rostov, and Helen Hindpere—the core creative team behind the game—were fired from ZA/UM, which they co-founded.  They allege they were ousted in a hostile corporate takeover orchestrated by investor Ilmar Kompus, who allegedly used funds from the studio’s profits to buy out the majority stake (including the original creators’ shares) through a shell company.  The key accusation is that Kompus acquired four concept sketches for a potential sequel (called Pioneer One) for just over €1, then resold them to ZA/UM for €4.8 million—effectively using studio money to buy the company from its creators.  In response, Kurvitz and Rostov filed lawsuits, claiming fraud, misappropriation of funds, and attempted IP theft.  ZA/UM denied wrongdoing, stating the creators were let go for poor performance, toxic behavior, and attempted IP sales, and that profits were reinvested into new projects.  The Estonian court has since seized Kompus’s stake to prevent its sale during legal proceedings.  The fallout has led to:  The cancellation of Disco Elysium 2. The firing of over a third of ZA/UM’s staff. A massive rift among fans, with some boycotting the game (and its merch) to protest the creators being cut off from profits. The original team urging fans to play pirated or borrowed copies and avoid supporting the current company, as they no longer have control or financial benefit from the game’s success. Despite the chaos, the legal battle is ongoing, and the future of the franchise remains uncertain.  The original creators maintain they are fighting to reclaim the artistic legacy they built over two decades.

text: Disco Elysium came very highly recommended. The best narrative cRPG of all time, the Torment-slayer. I kept hearing such comments from all directions. So much so that I broke my primary game-purchasing rule. The one that says, never buy a game until 6 months after release. A rare occurrence but, well, if this game was that good, I had to see for myself. It goes without saying I started this game with my expectations floating a bit over the stratosphere. But is this game really the next point of reference for fans of the genre, does it really deserve all this acclaim? Let's see.  The game starts strong. You wake up in a ruined motel room. Having apparently drunk your memories away. Quickly you realize you are a detective investigating a gruesome murder, all that in the middle of a major workers' strike and a looming greater social conflict. The atmosphere is strong and successfully manages to make you doubt everything and everyone. I soon started forming some pretty outlandish scenarios in my mind as to what was happening. For better or worse I was dead wrong and things though still twisty were a fair bit more pedestrian. The point is the narrative is engaging and like in any good murder mystery it keeps you guessing. At the same time, without spoiling anything, I will say that the story breaks several cardinal rules of detective fiction. While that can be excused as the game being a deconstruction, or even lauded as brave, those rules exist for a reason. They work. Indeed, the plot's resolution feels rather cheap. This makes the finale somewhat unsatisfying despite the excellent personal drama on display.  The setting is a world fairly similar to our own in the recent past. There is extensive world-building, done mostly via dialogue. There is also a lot of politics. Communism, fascism, moralism, feminism, racism and more are discussed extensively and the protagonist can embrace one or more of these ideologies. Admittedly this is done rather clumsily, an amnesiac that has no memory of what money is becoming a communist firebrand is not very convincing. Unfortunately, I'm not sure the world is different enough from our own to warrant being a wholly fictional setting, rather than being per se an Earth plus. It definitely makes it more difficult to follow all these politics. A good example of this is the racist character explaining racist theory to you and going on this long tirade about all those fictional races you absolutely can't place in context. The races being fictional serves no tangible purpose. It makes it almost feel like a cop-out to avoid offense. A costly cop-out.  Mechanically speaking there is a lot more narrative than there is game. There is no combat system for instance, or any other significant gameplay system, just dialogue. The character creation is straightforward. Four abilities governing a number of quirky skills. Creating effectively three types of detective, the physical, the instinctual and the rational type. Those skills are used to improve your odds against numerous skill checks throughout the game that determine the options you have available. Whether you pass a skill check depends on your skill points and the roll of the dice. Dice is a great way to add randomness in a PnP, but on a PC game they usually lead simply to save-scumming. This game makes an earnest effort to mitigate that issue. It gives interesting outcomes to failures that can take you down different paths. Or at least it tries to. It's not always very successful and there are skill checks you simply have to pass if you want to advance the plot. And back to save-scumming we go.  A controversial fact concerning the game's strong narrative is the player's inability to derail it. The game's story is effectively set. The bigger in scope events are in motion. They can't be changed. In fact after a point there even is a time limit. The player's agency is limited to how much of what's happening behind the scenes they can discover and whether they will solve the core case or not. No matter your choices, you won't change which political faction wins, you won't change the events that triggered the protagonist's fall. The scope is narrow, at best you will win a small, bittersweet victory and live to fight another day. No more. Arguably this is not a flaw of this game in particular, but more of a fundamental aspect of the genre. It would be next to impossible for a narrative to remain tight if the player could walk all over it. Nevertheless it does dampen the enthusiasm when making those choices somewhat.  Technically the game is surprisingly competent in its simplicity. Often being an indie release is a byword for a cheapskate production. Not here. The graphics were beautiful for what they were and the music/ambiance did its job fine. Voice overs were great when present. Unfortunately a great deal of dialogue is not voiced. I guess it would be too much to expect considering the amount. Still a shame though. The inventory system left me with mixed feelings. I certainly liked the books and generally the items you could interact with and I did appreciate the amount of clothing available, it allows you to customize your character a great deal. Unfortunately though it's not all cosmetic. Clothes give you skill boosts. Different ones. Cue in the clumsy ritual of having to put on the right outfit before every skill check. The game could have done without that.  To conclude, I probably came off more critical than necessary. Great expectations can have that effect. Fact is, this is a good game. While I don't really believe it will become the next point of reference when it comes to narrative cRPGs or that it slays any sacred cows. It is indeed a rare title with lots of interesting ideas. Surprisingly it is also the first game this team developed. I am very curious to see what they do next. Until then, I strongly recommend Disco Elysium to every fan of narrative-focused games out there.

text: This game should not exist... And I mean that in the best way possible. A game like this is a pipe dream at best and a delusion at worst. This game takes preconceptions of what games of a specific genre should be and throws them out a window. I found it hard to understand what the game was from the reviews and after playing it I know why. It's hard to explain what this game is without falling into the trap of shortselling it and making understatements. This game NEEDS to be played by anyone that remotely likes not only RPGs by any kind of agency in videogames... This game is the new standard by which any games that claims "choice matters" will be compared to forever.  The next generation of gamers will talk about Disco Elysium as the previous does about Planescape Torment and Fallout. This game should not exist, but I'm extremely grateful to the geniuses that made it happen for making sure it does.

text: I'd call Disco Elysium the greatest RPG I've ever played, and along with that quite possibly the most unapologetically human game that I know of. A biting, fiercely authentic experience about life that I wasn't quite convinced games could achieve. Was I ever so wrong.   You'll play the story of someone who has hit rock bottom - a police detective who has deeply, deeply screwed up and has been written off as hopeless by everyone that knows him. A walking disaster of such magnitude that you've drugged and drunken yourself into amnesia, with nothing to live for except a case you've been assigned to find the culprits behind a lynching, along with one steadfast companion by the name of Kim Kitsuragi. It's your job to catch the killer as fast as you can, allowing some of the life brimming in the city of Revachol to renew you along the way, or letting this chance all go to waste too and continue your abyssal plunge.  Right from the get-go, I’ll start off with the game’s central mechanical conceit - a total lack of combat in a text-based RPG. A lot of people will balk at the prospect of this, as I did, initially. However, what this actually does is remove the fluff and instead allows the game to bare itself for what it really is - a living novel that is an absolute joy to experience, replete with dialogue that kept me deeply engaged. How, exactly?  The game’s 24 skills aren't simply used to determine how good you are at killing foes, but instead each represent an aspect of your character - broadly divided into Intellect, Psyche, Physique, and Motorics - giving their take on the world: why that look in their eye? What's with their cadence and manner of speech? What's their game, what're they hiding? Who might be on their mind? What are they aching for? And what’s the environment like? How does it feel to exist in the world of Revachol? They'll even contradict each other sometimes! It makes for a textual experience far more immersive and richly detailed than most RPGs could dream of.  And making the text even more endlessly replayable and varied, along with differing skillsets, is the game’s novel Thought Cabinet - a system that allows you to internalize certain characteristics to feature in how you interact the game’s world characters. For example, I ended up as a communist art critic bisexual hobo cop through this, which ended up manifesting itself in the least expected places (and is just a great phrase to say on its own).  You’ll use these skills and Thoughts to take in the city of Revachol around you with its crushed dreams and worn hopes, and in conversations heavily. And what a range of conversations you’ll have! Every single NPC feels like a real person with meaningful depth. Every. Single. One. And every single one of the conversations you have with them is an absolute delight, encompassing so many emotions, from the darkly hilarious, to the philosophically contemplative, to the achingly sad, to the downright bizarre that you could only find in this game. During them, the smallest of choices and details return dozens of hours later, little reminders that keep the conversations so immersive and for once making you feel like your actions really do reverberate through the game's world.  Everything other aspect of Disco Elysium enhances its literary soul to allow it to become a well and true masterpiece. The soundtrack by Sea Power is wonderful, and even transcendent - it can simultaneously feel meditative, or peppy, and at the same time has an air of being worn-out and even bleak. It fits the game unbelievably well. The artstyle, much like the rest of the game, manages to be simultaneously consistently grounded and fantastically expressive. And the amazing voice acting and top-notch audio design make the fantastic writing all the more engaging to take in. You can hear the spaces, sighs, and coughs of the dialogue together with all the characters and layers hinted at by the text expressed wonderfully by the voicing; you'll hear the tinny echoing of an old receiver, or the static of a radio. It adds so much to the experience and makes me delighted we got the Final Cut.  I’d love to talk about all the range of interactions I had with the incredible, well-realized world of Disco Elysium, but I would want you to experience them on your own even more, so I'll end here.  Even if I could gripe about it being more beholden to RPG design structure than I'd like from an otherwise revolutionary game (you can repeat dialogue options even when fairly different responses are offered, you're encouraged to constantly change clothes for checks, save scumming is rendered incredibly easy to do) Disco Elysium is a truly landmark title and a passionate cry from the depths of human experience, put into prose. It's one of the incredibly rare games whose number I could count with my fingers that came along and truly rocked my world, setting my mind aflight and my heart aflame; it makes me feel blessed to be able to see my favorite medium grow and develop.   P.S.: I really love being able to swap between two languages on the fly in such a well-written game as someone trying to gain fluency in a second language, and seriously wish more text-heavy games had this feature.

text: A magical realism detective narrative set in a universe where both the punishment and reward for your depravity and debauchery is unrelenting existential despair, you filthy, brilliant masochist.   Primordial voices argue on infinite loop about your greatest human failures while you traverse a complex and nuanced political and socioeconomic landscape that pits capital against commoner, corruption against corruption, as a void of static cracks open in the briny sea and expands to swallow the whimper of war-torn humanity. Put on your best fucking tracksuit and gator boots, boost those intangibles, have an original thought for once, you Wasteland King, and roll the red 20-sider on solving the murder of a vanity-tattooed war criminal. Speak to his bloated corpse. Listen to his fat tongue and bulging eyes swaying from a tree-turned-playground-turned-gallows explain the afterlife. Vomit at the foot of his altar.  Remember who you were. Why she left. Face each twisting knife of your past as if you're living it for the first time. Decide who you are. Pay for *all* the damage you've done, you unrepentant narcissist. Apologize. Apologize.  Start an EDM dance-club drug-den with teens who proselytize the way of HARDCORE in an abandoned church where the stained-glass portrait of your Matron stares you into submission and a vagrant swings from the rafters to the highest point of the steeple to live where sound ceases.  There’s no task too tertiary to your investigation, you cryptid-loving communard, you magnesium-obsessed Capitalist. You contain fucking multitudes, moron.   Warm up those karaoke pipes and croon the saddest song in your heart and pray to the stained-glass portrait of a genocidal goddess someone finally sees you—not the dehydrated amphetamine-eaten hack, but a vastness of love, an embarrassment of spiritual riches. The worst fucking detective in the RCM. The best fucking detective in the RCM. A true child of Martinaise.  You control everything. You control nothing. Submit to your limbic system and play the void like your life depends on it. It does.

text: I believe that the best thing about this game is that no matter how hard you try to not screw things up, you end up screwing them. And God forbid that you try to mess everything and everyone up, you end up helping the most unexpected individual or group of people out there. text: Disco Elysium feels terrifyingly [b]real[/b]. It reminds you of the hard truth that existence can be a headache. Throughout your life, you're mostly sad and alone. You might feel like some of your memories are brutally unforgiving. Burdened by a world trying to tear you apart, you try to get by. Still, you always come back to the same old question: Why? What's the purpose of all this? And the game answers in all seriousness: [i]"There is no purpose. You're all alone. Everything is insignificant. Just give up."[/i] It's the heavy truth handed to you by the game like a hard-to-swallow pill.  Of course, nobody can pinpoint what this game is mainly about. Psychology, the inner workings of our mind? Philosophy, the meaning of life? Finding your identity when you feel like you're all alone in the world? Politics and ideologies? The moral of this game can be interpreted in a lot of ways but I think there's an obvious message it's trying to convey: [b]Being right doesn't exist.[/b] No matter what you think or do, it seems like everything is simply wrong. And when you try to choose a side or develop an opinion about something, the game critisizes you harshly. It defines you. But it also makes you change your outlook on life. You become more skeptical about yourself, making you question your beliefs. Although, in this game, even your own mind isn't a safe or trustworthy place. You can try to ignore your thoughts but they are too loud.  However, if you stop focusing on an end goal - in this case, why you came to Revachol in the first place - for even just a second, you can make living worthwhile and life beautiful. Explore yourself and get sidetracked from the main case, make the best moments by seeing what makes *you* feel like you. By having small conversations with the locals and paying attention to details you can truly enjoy life and come to a conclusion about your identity. In all honesty, solving the case might have been the worst part of the game because it ended it.

text: Disco Elysium is transcendent. I can't recommend it enough. Anyone who knows how to work a computer mouse should play this and see it through.  The world on display in this game never stops being fascinating. Every minute detail: its history, culture, politics, hell, even shockingly verbose fiction-within-the-fiction. I loved every piece of world-building, every minute detail, every corner of its streets. All this is elevated tenfold by the phenomenal soundtrack, which complements every piece of scenery in ways I may never be able to fully appreciate.   And all that goes without getting into the characters. My goodness, these characters. So much care has gone into fleshing out every single person you encounter in this adventure. No-one is without their history, their values, their heritage. This game is chock-full of living, breathing souls.  This is the height of story-telling in an interactive medium. In my life I've experienced countless works from several mediums, and nothing else has come close to matching Disco Elysium's effortless prose. Each bit of its script weaves a story as thorough as it is complex. Its simpler, more rudimentary graphical presentation may not be able to match the biggest advancements in the industry these days, but the words, music, and artwork surrounding it will brand an image crystal clear enough to surpass anything strictly attempting photorealism. And this has everything to do with the trust it holds for the player's own imagination. It presents so much more stimuli than words alone ever could, but holds back just enough to allow the script to carry it further still.  I'm fresh off my first playthrough, which I took entirely at my own pace, so everything I've said here is purely reactionary. But I believe these words to be true. You should buy this game for any price that's in front of you, and sit down to take it all in, just like you would a good novel.

text: It has been short of 27 hours and I'm really sad that it's over. This has been one of the best gaming experiences in my life and I am longing, nay, pining for a sequel or an expansion. Anything, just let me get back in there!   Disco Elysium is a narrative driven isometric Detective-RPG for adults. It has a bit of a Sci-Fi touch but is mostly dealing with darker adult topics (addiction, existential dread, failure in life, murder, politics etc.) in a fictional, pseudo-realistic world.  Despite all the doom and gloom it is also one of the funniest games I've ever played. It had me laughing out loudly within the first hour, the writing is just soooo good! I don't want to tell you much about the story, just know that I can barely remember being that invested in a videogame story. You play a cop who is trying to solve a murder in a crapsack world, that's all you need to know beforehand.  Gameplay consists mainly of exploring, talking and developing your character. There is no *real* combat system, so don't expect to put points in "Single-handed weapons" or something like that; instead you have skills like "Authority", "Hand-Eye-Coordination", "Logic" etc. These skills are constantly being checked in all kinds of situations (dialogues, exploration, using stuff in the world). It gets even deeper than that since clothing, drugs, previous actions and even "thoughts" can influence the outcome.   Depending on your skills and choices (so many choices!) you might experience a completely different playthrough than someone else, and here lies one of the greatest things about DE, something I've been missing from most recent "old-school" RPGs: You can really roleplay here! Develop the main char in any direction you want, physically, morally, fashion-wise etc. Since combat does not really play a role you can customize your Character far beyond the usual combat focus. I truly hope other devs take an example here!  I would love to recommend this to everybody, alas, I cannot. If you don't like reading in games, this is not for you, because this is what you will be doing 80% of the time. Reading, reading, reading. The writing is superb, accompanied by great sound design and decent voice actors (it's not fully voiced, though), but there is a *lot* of it. You have been warned.  If you like RPGs, can live without combat, love a really, really good story and enjoy reading, don't hesitate any longer. This is the game for you. I knew after the first hour that this will be one of my all-time-favorites and it kept it's promises all the way through. Thank you, ZA/UM!

You play a cop who is trying to solve a murder in a crapsack world, that's all you need to know beforehand.  Gameplay consists mainly of exploring, talking and developing your character. There is no *real* combat system, so don't expect to put points in "Single-handed weapons" or something like that; instead you have skills like "Authority", "Hand-Eye-Coordination", "Logic" etc. These skills are constantly being checked in all kinds of situations (dialogues, exploration, using stuff in the world). It gets even deeper than that since clothing, drugs, previous actions and even "thoughts" can influence the outcome.   Depending on your skills and choices (so many choices!) you might experience a completely different playthrough than someone else, and here lies one of the greatest things about DE, something I've been missing from most recent "old-school" RPGs: You can really roleplay here! Develop the main char in any direction you want, physically, morally, fashion-wise etc. Since combat does not really play a role you can customize your Character far beyond the usual combat focus. I truly hope other devs take an example here!  I would love to recommend this to everybody, alas, I cannot. If you don't like reading in games, this is not for you, because this is what you will be doing 80% of the time. Reading, reading, reading. The writing is superb, accompanied by great sound design and decent voice actors (it's not fully voiced, though), but there is a *lot* of it. You have been warned.  If you like RPGs, can live without combat, love a really, really good story and enjoy reading, don't hesitate any longer. This is the game for you. I knew after the first hour that this will be one of my all-time-favorites and it kept it's promises all the way through. Thank you, ZA/UM!

text: Review is based on two thorough playthroughs, with wildly different character builds and dialogue choices in each.  There's two halves to Disco Elysium: a video game, and a role-playing experience.  The game is a point-and-click detective RPG without combat. The game is built on active and hidden passive dice rolls in a series of conversations - with other people and inanimate objects - all corresponding to different aspects of your personality in place of standard stats and skills. It's unique and intriguing to play a game that is itself a deep dive into the player character's psychology, with a 'fail forward' approach to failed rolls that makes failure (almost) fully accounted for and fun to see the results of. It takes place in a story about a city trampled under neoliberalism, and how people live with that reality. It's a story about being confronted with crushing inequality as an outsider, about questioning your own role as someone who enforces that inequality, about living with personal and political heartbreak, about trying to fight for your sobriety when the world drives you to alcohol and drug abuse. Despite the 'choices matter' tag, they honestly don't; you'll almost assuredly arrive at the exact same conclusion, but that tag speaks to the strength of the illusion.  And that's where the role playing experience comes in.  Though the story is, mostly, pretty heavily linear, the journey matters so much more than the destination. After finishing the first playthrough that left me in tears, proud of my empathetic, apologetic cop starting his path to clean living and moving on, I came back months later, to start a playthrough as a physical, aggressive fascist whose only understanding of social skills was 'I am a cop, I am a god'. And that's when the game got its claws in me all over again.  It was this second playthrough when it really set in for me that Disco Elysium truly is an RPG instead of a visual novel with dicerolls attached. That illusion of choice is strong because of the range of self-expression that the game's dialogue trees generally allow. I absolutely [i]despised[/i] my second character, but I was enthralled by the performance art that playing the game became, watching a story evolve where he developed a crippling addiction to magnesium antidepressants to offset the morale lost from alcohol and racist rants. It's a game that knows how to be both funny and emotional in equal measure (albeit not without its own pitfalls), and I'm excited to have a third playthrough after a couple months of 'cooling off' before starting a playthrough as another type of detective.  Absolutely, completely recommended. Oh, and show that phrenologist who's boss.

text: Disco Elysium. A game about Communism, Capitalism, Liberals, Unions, Social Democracy, Monarchism, Genocide, Suicide, Natural law, Empathy and Hope.  It shows us how stubborn old men cling to their past and pride, allowing the long gone days to dictate their very belief's and words to taint the world before them with hate and fanaticism.  It shows us how young credulous souls suffer in silence because the adults who promised to built a better world so that those after them may live a better life than they did, failed.  It shows how refusing to live in the present and instead drown yourself in the past moulders the soul. It shows the story of a man burying away his memories comes face to face with the consequences of his self destructive tendencies and self neglect. I could go on on how the game wonderfully explores and masterfully demonstrates different subjects like the human enigma, psychology, affective science, politics, ideologies.. but I instead will likely remember the game for one thing.  The bug. The stick bug that gave me a glimpse into it's life and made me envious of how she lives her desolate life, incapable of identifying with abstractions and how the concept of nothingness is a unique human quality as her very exsistence demands she lives day to day. Her biggest worry is simply to make it to tomorrow. And yet in her heart, however small it may have been. She offered me empathy. She gave me hope. She made me glad to be who I am, made me glad to be me.    Disco Elysium is a vision of hope offered by existentialism. To know that the world is indifferent, that nothingness lurks within and around you, and yet not to flinch. To know there is no essential truth, only choices you can make, most of them painful, most of them wrong. And yet, despite that knowledge, to wake up to the world and make those choices anyway. Day after day. Second by second.  I exist. And tomorrow, something beautiful is going to happen.

text: This has unironically changed my brain chemistry.  I tried it once YEARS ago, didn't immediately get a handle on the skill points/thought cabinet, and put it down. Coming back and trying again, going "Just do it, who cares, if you do things wrong its fine, just dive in" and I'd like to say that was possibly the perfect was to start the game.    You may not "get it" immediately, you may feel foolish as you try to ground yourself, and maybe you become emotionally dependent on Kim Kitsuragi.  That's all okay, I dare say its intended, and you are all the better in the shoes of the main character who is just as or MORE lost than you are.

text: Like all good detective stories, what appears simple at first becomes so much more than that in Disco Elysium – and here it gets so, so much weirder, too. It takes the age-old mechanics of tabletop RPGs like Dungeons & Dragons and twists them in strange ways around a macabre tale of violence, poverty, and a society on the brink of collapse. Through sharply written dialogue and an expertly crafted world, it uses some unique game mechanics - such as debating against 24 different sections of your own brain - to create a story that will stay with me for a long time. And, somehow, it manages to make all of this fun and, surprisingly often, funny. Now with the addition of a fully voiced cast and even more side quests to embark on, The Final Cut makes an amazing game even better.  The premise of Disco Elysium is straightforward: A body has been discovered, hanged from a looming tree in the backyard of a hostel, and it’s up to you to work out how it got there over the course of the 30-hour story. Everything that surrounds this core mystery is far from simple, however, not least being that you kick things off with an almighty dose of hangover-induced amnesia. You can’t even remember your name, let alone that you are a cop on a murder case. A part of your consciousness described as your ancient reptilian brain – which you literally engage in conversation with – attempts to persuade you to give up your quest even as your snivelling limbic system battles against it. As you stumble around your wrecked bedroom searching for remnants of your former self, it quickly becomes clear that this isn’t simply a whodunnit, but a journey that will challenge you to solve crises on both profoundly personal and societal levels. It’s a gorgeously designed isometric RPG that makes you think at every turn of its painterly streets.

text: [h1][i]"Real darkness has love for a face. The first death is in the heart."[/i][/h1]  TLDR: There's a short[i]ish[/i] summary at the bottom of this monstrosity. An urgent suggestion: Don't spoil yourself with videos or screenshots about this game, you'll ruin your first and inimitable playtrough and experience.  Disco Elysium has such an unique and poetic way to portray the mind and life of an amnesic, alcohol addicted cop and its aftermath with so much melancholy, that it was easy to sympathize or identify yourself with the protagonist. Or at least an extraordinary introduction of a broken mind or even a bizarre political argument, especially with low rhetoric. And while playing, even as an amnesic cop, you still have to investigate to solve a case you've actually forgotten about, like everything else, your name for example, and you catch yourself wondering [i]"Do I even want to know what happened? Or who I really am? Oh my god, did I really do that??"[/i]. Well, here's the reason why I recommend this deeply emotional experience.  Talking, walking around and inspecting things, reading a book to pass some time, put some clothes on to look like an idiot but pass an important conversation about economics, another round of talking with people, questioning, invenstigating, talking to yourself, just talking and reading for hours are your [b]only[/b] activities in this game.  This probably is a big PASS for a huge amount of gamers, because it's a different kind of role playing. You're using your skills and consciousness as your weapon, with skill checks tied to them. Suppose we don't want this to be easy.   I would strongly recommend it if you're already into visual novel games, but the game tags on the store page do describe the type of gameplay and what to expect really good. Don't buy it because it's "hyped" and then end up writing a negative review because you "had to read so much and nothing else" and actually check the store page.  While people do explain that this game has no combat, I want to slightly disagree regarding to the different perspective of what actually counts as combat. Because our protagonist [b]does[/b] fight, constantly I have to emphasize, for his own identity or to restore oneself. Against or with 24 different skills, all having their own thoughts, interests and needs. Already thinking about how to satisfy them all? Have fun trying.  You can spend your skill points into physique, like endurance, to have a better chance fighting against this harsh world you woke up in. Or how about a lot of points into intellect? Everyone loves and respects a rational, analytic and intelligent cop, right? Sounds like an easy job, well done.  Imagine you did as I said and didn't spend any points in empathy, for example?  [h1][i]"How long had he been there?" Empathy: "If you say 'two days maybe' it will be etched in her mind forever."[/i][/h1]  The dialogues adapt to the level of your skills, some conversations may turn out differently if you fail the skill checks (which are tied to the skills and can be increased while leveling up or wearing clothes with the wanted bonus) or some don't even show up.  Sometimes you'll have regrets about following your highest skill, because, similar to real life, logic isn't always the best answer and you can't take your words back. Sometimes you can't even retry a failed skill check (yes I'm talking about those 97% success chances I've failed a dozen times, thank you game).  So you're getting the experience to deal and fight with the protagonists consciousness and its impact on the world and people around you.  As I mentioned, your consciousness, or in fact your 24 skills, have a different mind, different thoughts and different demands, all wanting to be heard and satisfied, trying to lure you from the path you may want to follow with their tempting ideas for different thoughts to research and gain new information or improve your skills. Or maybe change your personality, not always in a pleasant way or how you originally imagined.  Slight conversation spoiler for an example:  I had a hard time with the encyclopedia skill, because I pushed it really high and it bugged me almost constantly in every conversation with enormous text blocks or unwanted, actually unnecessary information! While this also turned the protagonist into some kind of snob, it was especially tiring to try and follow 4 single thoughts at once - while still investigating and following the main story!  [i]You: "What's a 'contact microphone'?" Acele: "A contact mic records sounds from inside things. Like this ice." Encyclopedia [Easy: Success]: "Your mangled brain would like you to know there is a boxer called Contact Mike."  You: "What am I supposed to do with this?"  Encyclopedia: "No idea."[/i]   You may not be responsible for the amnesic alcoholic part, that's the protagonists past, but you're jointly responsible for his actions during the story and his behavior, who do you want him to be and if you can change him, allowing you to choose what your characters ideals are, what type of cop you are, aso. Or at least wondering how you managed to unlock thoughts like Hobocop, Homosexual Underground or Cop of the Apocalypse. You are holding the key to his mind in your hands.  [h1][i]It's like every time I'm talking to people I'm choosing Option D, 'none of the above'... Is that moralism?"[/i][/h1]  Another point I'd like to address: exploration. While you're probably going to try to talk to everyone and gain as much information and context as possible, you can't do everything and there's an increased chance with every passing day to miss some people or sidequests, be it because of the lack of money, time or low skills. Like I said, it's your responsibility to try and solve everything you want, the way you'd like it to turn out.   So, did I manage to persuade you? At least about the combat?   I do hope this unique game gets a sequel or the developers will continue making similar games, because they have shown their huge potential and creativity level. It has become one of my favorite games of all time I enjoy coming back to and still find new bits of dialogues.   We [b]need[/b] different, unique and outstanding rpg games like Disco Elysium to break out of this ever repeating chain of copy and paste or simplyfied games, even if it's a niche product. Thanks for reading!  >>>>>>>>> TLDR:  [h1][i]"The question is, what is the question?"[/i][/h1]  Pros:  + phenomenal detective story and storytelling + absolutely amazing dialogue system + interesting and unique characters with their own captivating stories + entertaining sidequests, I'm so glad I didn't miss Billie Méjean + the time mechanic and management, time passes when talking with somebody or reading a book, so you kind of have to plan your day, without pressure, who you want to talk with and what information to gain without wasting too much time, just like a real cop! + really good voice acting, which gives some thoughts and moments an outstanding touch + Kim Kitsuragi, just because + and Cuno while we're at it + different languages, this deserves his own mention, because actually being able to translate this mountain of words is admirable, I checked the german one briefly and was surprised how convincing and smooth it was + hours and hours of reading, you're [b]not[/b] doing much else, so if you don't like books or reading, don't buy! + the beautiful artstyle + Do you remember what happened when we tried to DANCE? I'm actually scared of my spinal cord  Cons:  - sometimes you'll need a dictionary or wikipedia (I sure did) to understand the current topic, especially during political arguments. While gaining a massive amount of information about fictional wars and places, it's hard to stay focused constantly - some thoughts in the thought cabinet could use a few more hints what they're actually about and what you'll gain when researching them

text: Normally, I'd stay away from anything that's as text-heavy as Disco Elysium is but, for whatever reason, the moment I laid my eyes on this game, I knew that it would be something that I don't want to miss.     Pros: [list] [*] This is an actual, full-fledged RPG. Not just a game with character progression. [*] Stellar writing. [*] Fantastic visuals. [*] Although lacking in quantity, there is no denying the quality of the soundtrack. [/list]   Cons: [list] [*] For a game with mostly pre-rendered background drops, this one is unusually unstable and choppy. [*] Despite all of the choice and consequence mechanics the ending seems to be mostly pre-determined. However, this is not really a huge deal as it’s the journey that counts, not the destination. [/list]    First of all, let me say that [b]Disco Elysium is NOT a game for everybody[/b] despite it being nothing but good through and through. [b]This is an EXTREME example of a niche title[/b] and if you don’t know what you’re getting, I ask of you to [b]do your research and see what the gameplay is all about[/b] before being pissed off about the game being too slow or text-heavy.  Just to make sure that we’re on the same page I’ll make it crystal-clear that Disco Elysium is primarily text-based. You will read a lot and then read some more until you move through the world so you can read something new.  With that being said, if you’re someone who appreciates a [i]true[/i] RPG gameplay with insane character creation, customization, and development in a world where everything your character does, says, and (quite literally) thinks, has a significant impact on the way the story develops, look no further and get Disco Elysium at full price because these developers deserve it!    [h2] Here’s What’s So Cool About It: [/h2] In Disco Elysium, your character has a total of 24 unique skills grouped and governed by four different attributes: Intellect, Psyche, Physique, and Motoric. Those 24 skills can be increased based on how developed the governing attribute for that skill is. So for example, a total of 5 points in Psyche will allow you to level the psyche-based skills up to 5 times.   On top of that, you can contemplate on certain things by acquiring thoughts as you progress through the game, engage in dialogues, observe the world around you or simply level up some skills past a certain point.    A combination of these abilities, skills, and thoughts will directly impact the way your character experiences and interacts with the game world and its inhabitants.  So, for example, a character focusing on Intellect will be able to have a high Encyclopedia which will allow them to produce massive amounts of information about pretty much everything regarding the game’s lore.   This knowledge can be very useful when talking to people, exploring the world, and working on your police case. But here’s where it gets interesting... Level up your Encyclopedia for too much and your character becomes [i]so knowledgeable that he’s boring both you, the player, as well as the NPC’s[/i] that he’s talking with. He’ll be constantly providing so much info on the most trivial and uninteresting topics that you might be tempted to skip through (although I really don’t advise this as it’s all part of the game’s design) and the characters around you might find it annoying which will impact their disposition towards you.   Furthermore, the game will present you with unique skill-based dialogue options that might seem like a good pick but, because your skill is too high, those might actually backfire on you at times and piss-off certain NPC’s.     [h2] The Verdict [/h2] Real choice and consequence system unlike any you’ve ever seen (or have you?) tied directly to the character progression system. If that’s not the foundation for a fantastic and unforgettable role-playing game, I don’t know what is.  Despite its seemingly pre-determined ending which feels a bit off in what is otherwise such a vastly branching game, Disco Elysium’s journey makes it all worth it and leaves me wanting for more.  In many ways, [i]it reminded me of one of my favorite games of all time, an RPG which raised the bar for me to an unreachable level which is yet to be surpassed[/i], and only certain titles like this one ever come close to – Vampire the Masquerade: Bloodlines. If you’re a fan of that one, you will most likely share my enthusiasm and love for this game so, by all means, get it.   P.S.  [i]Disco Elysium – The Final Cut[/i] has been announced and it promises an expanded world, more quests, NPC’s to chat with while taking advantage of the “full voice-acting", controller support, and additional language options so, if you’re not aching to play, maybe get it to support the developers but wait for that version to go live?

text: Disco Elysium is something special. RPG/Adventure game with absolutely astonishing writing and unique/fresh character system.   You play as detective who lost his memory; of everything... Waking up totally destroyed in a hotel room. *What happened?* you might ask. Sorry, won't spoil [i]that[/i] for you : )  ---  [b]Main features[/b]  Dialog system is heavily tied to your character statistics which makes all the dialogs engaging and fun. Not only you have to make the right choices (and they are not obvious most of the time - due to good writing) but also, your character perceives the world though his skills. They are "voices" of your subconsciousness which help you interpret the world around you.  You might not notice some hidden item due to low Perception. Or you might not get sarcastic joke due to low Drama and you will be locked out of certain conversation. There is 24 different skills in total, distributed in 4 categories which gives this system decent depth.   At the start of the game you assign basic level for your skills through the 4 categories and then improve them individually as the character gains new points in the game. Points are also spent to unlock new "thoughts" or "concepts" which you gain from conversations and critical decisions. You can research the "concepts" if u like and add them as passive skills.   Some of your actions will require a skill check which is <your stat> + variables + 2d6 roll. Difficulty varies. You can make some tough checks easier by acquiring additional information/details - depending on the situation.   ---  [b]This game totally destroyed me[/b]  - When I died 1st minute into the game (wtf lol) - When I was one step away from arresting certain person and I wasn't quite sure, like 90-95% but something didn't make sense. I was so torn apart that I had to rethink it for 20 minutes. No joke. Games don't do this very often. Few RPG does. - With Inland Empire and Shivers skills  !!SPOILER!! [spoiler]"LITTLE" FRIEND BUG <3[/spoiler] [spoiler]TRIBUNAL[/spoiler]  Beautiful game <3  EDIT: I just finished the game after 40 hours, almost 3 days straight. And I feel sad. Because I want more! Disco Elysium is *really* good. Like 10/10 good. Maybe even genre defining good? Can't wait for DLC/follow up title.

text: Easily my GOTY pick.  First playthrough took me about 44hrs, and that was with my task list still left fairly robust and incompletable with my chosen build. What's more to be said that the other thousands of Overwhelmingly Positive reviews haven't already covered? If you enjoy actual intelligent dialogue, a unique skill system which all have their own personas and personalities in your head vying for control, a success/failure skill system where failing actually leads to many new and possibly more lucrative outcomes, and adventure gaming/Planescape torment style RPG's then this is a must have. You'll laugh, and cry, and feel real emotions for this bumbling coked up drunk overweight 'hero' as he learns more about his past, the (absolutely stunning and lore rich) world around him, and the conspiracy of the investigation at hand.  My only sore spot is that this team and this game has pretty much ruined CRPG's and basic 'safe' writing in other games going forward unless they step up; since for the first time since Planescape Torment the bar has been raised once again.

text: Let me set the stage: you are playing Skyrim or Fallout and in your sidequest, a character makes reference to an another person in the world. You are curious, so you find another NPC to talk to about this person, and you even go search out the person they are talking about to ask them about what you heard. Chances are, you will never get the opportunity to do so because the choices you get in those games are not of any substance. Even if you make a connection in your head, you will never be able to have characters in the world acknowledge that connection. There is a limitation on the canned responses you get to make to other characters and sometimes, you don't get the option that reflects your opinion or the subject you want to talk about. It takes you out of the RPG side of those games and makes you feel like your time and critical thinking was all for nothing.   Enter Disco Elysium.   If you realize a connection between two topics, people, or events in this game, you will almost certainly have a dialogue option or world-interaction to reinforce that connection and get additional dialogue about it. The world feels alive and the puzzles don't always have a sidequest name. There are rewards for exploring and interacting with characters even when your current objective doesn't require it. I never felt like my opinion couldn't be expressed in one of the responses offered (other than in dialogue with a certain round character) and every decision you make (even ones that do not appear to be decisions) is reflected in either an interaction with a character or in an internal monologue. I love this game because even though I didn't get to pick the character's appearance, name, or backstory, I am able to put myself in his place. If you like reading and appreciate games that respond to your critical thinking skills, Disco Elysium is for you.

text: [i]Disco Elysium[/i] is a text heavy CRPG in the [i]Planescape Torment[/i] mould. With all that dialogue to [strike]read through[/strike] listen to, the writing really needed to be top notch. Fortunately that's the case here; the writing is superb. It's intelligent, creative, witty and engaging, all in equal measure. There were a few moments that went over my head, or had me skim reading when the politics got a little heavy, but mostly, I was along for the ride.   And what a ride it is.  Rebuild your shattered mind and body in this beautifully stylised, deeply immersive world, and maybe have a go at solving a murder while you're at it. The complex character system really impresses, allowing you to play a number of detective-like roles.  [b]Here's a short list of some of the things you can get up to during a play-through:[/b]  1. Have a heart attack whilst getting dressed. 2. Proposition a suspect. 3. Punch a child ([i]don't worry, he deserves it[/i]) 4. Debate morality and race with a xenophobic-nationalist. 5. Fail to knock out a xenophobic-nationalist. 6. Tie people up with your impressive logic. 7. Leap across buildings. 8. Breakdance. Become one with the music of the universe. Disco Elysium, baby! 9. Substance abuse. 10. Talk to yourself. 11. Argue with yourself. 12. Love yourself. 13. Substance abuse. 14. Karaoke. 15. Become a communist. 16. Become a capitalist. 17: Eat a sandwich! 18. Hunt for creatures unknown to science. 19. Solve complex bullet telemetry in your head. 20. Read a book. 21. Introspection. 22. Sleep. 23. Throw-up. 24. Substance abuse with some homeless men. 25. Play Boules with a veteran.... and much, much more.  If all that doesn't make you want to play, I don't know what will. Maybe try substance abuse?

text: a CRPG for people who prioritize writing & voice acting  - doesn't objectify morality - doesn't push you to min/max - doesn't force you to party with characters who have little to no reason for doing so  - you can go to the main story points, get a little distracted with side-quests, or experience hours of voiced interactions within your own head  by not allowing a choice for the main character, the game doesn't have to shoehorn a custom character into the story. it instead gives you great freedom in its stat system and the myriad of ways to approach most tasks. sometimes failing a check will result in the opportunity to make different checks, or even open an entirely new side quest.  fair warning: i'm not even sure if there's combat in this game, at least not that i've seen in my current playthrough. while i enjoy the tactical fights of more standard CRPGs (Pillars, Baldur's, Pathfinder, Fallout, Wasteland, etc), most of them lack the writing to keep me interested in the story.   i feel like they too often rely on world-building (good as it may be) and us wanting to upgrade things to push exploration, yet we end up playing through the same tropes in new locations, usually just trying to be "good" or "evil". Disco has you talking to your character's conscience as much as the other characters, which i feel results in a world of difference when it comes to immersion in their actions.  in conclusion: i recommend it as a solid piece of interactive literature made exceptional by great voice acting, intriguing art & sound designs, and fresh & unique world building

text: You can cajole an old man to join an ultranationalist vigilante group in an attempt to requisition his ham sandwich. You can paint cryptic murals in the middle of a murder investigation while your partner actively worries for your mental stability. You can help anodic proto-ravers set up a nightclub and drug lab in an abandoned church. Your necktie can tell you to be an anarchist and set people on fire. You can tell neoliberals to their faces that they'll be first against the wall in the revolution. Your base instincts can quote DMX songs at you. You can have a conversation with a bug about the scourge of humanity and the horrors of consciousness. You can die by sitting on a particularly uncomfortable chair.  I don't know what art is, but this is art.

text: I honestly don't like this kind of dialogue-heavy game.  Even in the dozens of RPGs I've played, I rarely paid that much attention to dialogue. Partly because some games subject you to endless walls of text, and partly because, when it comes to role-playing, the characters I create tend to have this attitude of, "Something happened in the world? Cool. Not my problem."  But Disco Elysium...  Wow. Just wow. Good lord.  I don't think I've ever read this much text in a game before. And why?  Because every single line, every sentence, every little corner of this game is meticulously crafted and packed with detail. The consequences, the successes, the failures, the way everything reacts to everything else...  I've had moments like this before. The sheer brilliance of Hollow Knight's map system. The level of realism in Red Dead Redemption 2. The incredible narrative cohesion of Baldur's Gate 2. I honestly wasn't sure whether I'd ever experience that kind of shock and admiration from a game again.  Then I played Disco Elysium.  And I f...ing loved it.  Even though I feel like I've done pretty much everything that can reasonably be done in a single playthrough, I'm absolutely certain that if I played this game a few more times, I'd have completely different experiences every time.  There was a scene in Naruto where Madara declared Might Guy to be the strongest taijutsu user.  Well, I hereby declare Disco Elysium to be a literary masterpiece of the gaming world: a game with an unparalleled depth of writing, a truly unique role-playing system, and an almost flawless narrative centered around human psychology.  You somehow got a man who is practically illiterate when it comes to reading dialogue to sit there for 30+ hours and read like a f....ng book worm.  And it didn't stop there.  You made me love it.  Then you made me feel guilty for not doing the game justice.  [b] 95/100 [/b]   **P.S. — A huge shout-out to Locpick and the entire Turkish localization team.**  Disco Elysium has roughly 1.2 million words, so localizing a game like this into Turkish must have been an absolutely enormous task. Knowing that a 20-person team spent around nine months working on the translation, proofreading, and localization QA makes the quality of the result even more impressive.  The Turkish localization is genuinely outstanding. Huge respect to everyone at Locpick who worked on it. You made this incredible game accessible to Turkish players without losing the depth and personality of its writing.

text: First of all - this is the best cRPG I have played to this day, for a variety of reasons.  Disco Elysium works the way a tabletop RPG in real life does: you can attempt to do something and you roll dice (2d6). You either succeed or fail. Rinse and repeat. All is done via text interface. It's as simple as that. But wait, that sounds boring, right?  Wrong.  Disco Elysium's strongest point are stats and the way they allow you to interact with the world... and you! Yes, you heard me right! (Or, rather, your read it in your mind correctly.) Your stats are not just a bunch of boring numbers. Your stats can talk to you, thus giving you insight and ideas you otherwise wouldn't have.  It's like hearing Prattchet's voice that speaks to you when you're reading a book and having a conversation with it. Only there are more voices than one, and they can even talk to each other, so it can be crowded at times. But it's also what makes the game hilarious.  It also helps present information as a dialogue, by breaking what would-be a wall of text down into smaller chunks that are much easier to swallow, rather than a giant monologue.   Another advantage of the stats is that they can offer you their – unasked for – advice and help with doing things you are trying to accomplish (generally you [b]WANT[/b] to succeed while attempting the skill checks), and that's another reason why Disco is great cRPG: your stats impact what you're doing.  But there is more. It's hard to have all skills at high level, so you are bound to miss some things, while you're discovering others. Since you won't gain knowledge that your character won't obtain - due to having not high enough skills - you won't be able to act on it. Not only this means more replayability, but also helps to keep things in-character in a way that feels natural to the player. As far as I am aware no cRPG was able to accomplish a feat like this before.  As if that wasn't enough, having highly leveled stat isn't just a positive. Stats may start pushing you do things that may or may not be beneficial to you as a player/character and the higher they are, the more influence they will have. It's a brilliant way to stimulate internal conflicts and stuff like addictions of the character you're playing as.  I was having a lot of fun with the game (well, I still am!) and that's largely thanks to how seamlessly the text-based interactions combine with the automatic dice-rolling and personified skills constantly interjecting to give you their input. Despite the game boiling down to pure reading, it manages to grab your attention and suddenly you realize you've spent hours looking at the screen, having fun. Imagine that!  The writting itself is very good too. Like I said before, I found myself laughing a lot during these first few 6-7 hours and I expect myself to laugh even more in the future. I think that whoever did the text was really enjoying what he was doing. Or maybe it's just that the game's humour happens to resonate particularly strongly with me. The game is throwing punches left, right and center. No ideology is safe and nothing is sacred. Literally.  So, yeah, personally I think this game is a must-have for anyone who considers himself a fan of the RPG genre. And even if you aren't one, there is still a pretty high chance you will like it anyway.  If you don't trust me, trust the voices in your head.

text: Writing a short review of Disco Elysium feels like a fool’s errand. I suppose there’s an alternate universe in which the game is a hidden gem rather than a breakthrough success, but it’s hard to imagine; it’s so self-confident, so willing to be straight-up literary in a way few videogames even try to be, and so ambitious in its radical reimagining of the isometric RPG, that it seems destined to spread by word-of-mouth. In many ways it reminds me of Kentucky Route Zero, which is about the highest praise I can give to a game, much less one by first-time developers.  The most obvious difference between Disco and every other RPG is that there’s no combat engine; every conflict is resolved by skill checks, including any violence that may emerge. The skills themselves are also unusual; instead of “lockpicking” or “melee weapons,” you have “inland empire" (to help you see the hidden truths beyond reality, David Lynch style) and “visual calculus” (to help you reconstruct crime scenes). In addition, high levels of skills are not always good; I raised my “Encyclopedia” stats very high, allowing me to recall all sorts of useful information, but also leaving my character obsessed with trivia that wasn’t relevant to anything.  This system allows players to build their protagonist how they want without worrying about “trap builds'', the total opposite of traditional RPGs like Pathfinder. The mechanics couldn’t be simpler: every attempted action in the game does a skill check with the relevant skill, which is simply rolling two six-sided dice and adding the skill’s value. But it’s such a flexible system that it allows the designers to come up with interesting and novel uses of skills, and ensures that each playthrough of Disco Elysium is substantially different.  The other distinguishing feature of Disco Elysium is just how dense it is. The entire game takes place within a relatively small neighborhood; I’ve honestly never played an RPG with so small a map. But this is more than counterbalanced by the sheer number of characters to interact with, interiors to explore, and mysteries to solve. It's probably the closest thing I've seen to Warren Spector's "one city block" design. And you do this all as a complete mess of a cop, struggling with his sanity and the decisions he has made. It’s a welcome break from being the chosen one.  It’s hard to write about Disco Elysium without making it sound like a difficult art game, the sort of thing you might admire more than enjoy, but it’s surprisingly accessible, and it never talks down to its audience; it’s not interested in dropping references to erudite works, but in embodying their best features. And the protagonist's partner, Lt. Kim, is both a source of help when you get stuck, and perhaps the best “companion” character I’ve seen in an RPG (complete with absolutely top-notch voice acting by someone with zero previous credits to their name).  Last, but certainly not least, Disco Elysium is very, very funny, and allows the player to lean more and more into the absurdities they encounter if they wish; as someone who usually “plays it straight,” I often found myself pursuing chaotic approaches just to see what would happen, and was never disappointed. This is a highly reactive RPG, that pulls from a seemingly infinite script to tailor the experience to your character’s skills and flaws.  There’s a lot more to write about (the method of unlocking memories and ideas that influence your character; the brilliant, haunting soundtrack by band British Sea Power; the absolutely stellar pacing), but it’s safe to say that Disco Elysium is one for the ages. Many of my favorite video games are already largely obscure and forgotten, and are hard sells to a modern audience less willing to put up with their antiquated designs. But I’m confident people will still be discovering and playing Disco Elysium for many decades.
